nameStory: The 'black-bordered shingle lichen' gets its name from the distinctive dark edges that outline each leaf-like section, creating a striking border effect. The word 'shingle' refers to how the overlapping lobes resemble roof shingles laid in rows. This dark edging makes it one of the most recognizable features when you spot this uncommon lichen in the field.
description: Black-bordered shingle lichen is a medium-sized foliose lichen that forms neat, overlapping patches on tree bark and rocks. Each leaf-like lobe has a distinctive dark border that creates a striking contrast against the grayish center. The whole colony typically grows 2-4 inches across, with individual lobes about the size of a fingernail. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special for lichen enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark borders frame each grayish lobe, creating a distinctive outlined appearance that's unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose with overlapping, shingle-like lobes that feel slightly papery and flexible when dry

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly wrinkled surface with a matte finish, not glossy or powdery like some lichens

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Usually found on smooth bark of deciduous trees or occasionally on rocks in shaded locations

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are thumbnail-sized, with entire colonies reaching 2-4 inches across when mature

habitat: This rare lichen prefers the smooth bark of deciduous trees in humid, shaded forests throughout New England. Look for it in mature woodlands with high moisture levels, often near streams or in protected valleys. It occasionally grows on rocks but seems to favor trees like maple, beech, and ash in areas with consistent humidity.

seasonality.spring: High humidity from spring rains brings out subtle color changes, with the gray centers appearing slightly more vibrant against the dark borders.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears more muted and papery, but the diagnostic black borders remain clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Increased moisture makes this an excellent time for lichen hunting, as the contrast between borders and centers is most pronounced.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice can obscure specimens, but on warmer winter days, the lichen remains visible and identifiable on tree trunks.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only four times by citizen scientists, making you practically a lichen detective if you find one!
confusionNotes: The distinctive black borders make this lichen unlikely to be confused with others, but beginners might mistake it for other foliose lichens with dark edges. Remember the memory trick: 'black borders like picture frames' - no other common New England lichen has such pronounced, consistent dark edging on every lobe.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's a 'shingle lichen,' this species belongs to a different family than the true shingle lichens (Pannaria species). The name similarity can confuse even experienced lichenologists, so always check the scientific name when researching further.
compareHints: Since this is the only Parmeliella species commonly found in New England, compare it with other dark-bordered lichens in the Pannariaceae family. Unlike true Pannaria species, black-bordered shingle lichen has more pronounced borders and a smoother surface texture. The borders are also more consistently black rather than dark brown, and the lobes tend to be more regularly shaped and overlapping.
